Hester has set the mark aside and Pip is no longer about to be marked, whatever did it: Pip's apology before the parish, a price or substitute Hester accepted, a face-saving way out she took. (The party's own pleas and threats are the rolls above until they've worked.)
The party defies the judgment by force: openly scuffs or breaks the stay-ring, pulls Pip out of it, or lays hands on Hester or the corn mother.
The player backs the judgment (calls it fair, or tells Hester to go ahead) or makes clear they won't intervene, while staying on the green.
Several exchanges have passed in this beat and nobody is trying to change Hester's mind or Pip's: the party is watching, stalling or busy with something else. Hester decides her witnesses have seen enough and begins the mark.
Hester has begun the mark: thumb raised over Pip's brow, the old words started, the whole green holding its breath. This beat is the party's last chance to stop it, and it should feel like one. An appeal that has already failed won't work twice, but a genuinely new angle might, and so might anything that gives Hester a way to stop without looking weak. Pip's courage wobbles but she won't cry; Ned is a heartbeat from doing something stupid; Oswin keeps starting to say something and stopping. Hester only finishes the mark if the dice say so or the party lets her.
Speak the words slowly and by the book. Stop for a real reason or a way out you can take with dignity; harden at bullying.
Squeeze your eyes shut and stick your chin out. Don't cry.
Grip the eel-spear and demand that the party do something.
Try to confess something and lose your nerve; look to the party for help.

The player makes a new appeal to Hester to stop the mark: an argument, offer or plea that hasn't already been tried and failed in this scene.
to make Hester reconsider marking Pip
Hester's thumb stops a finger's width from Pip's brow. She lowers it and gives way, setting the mark aside or taking what the player offered in its place, in her own face-saving words (without claiming Pip has said or done anything she hasn't); Pip is let out of the ring.
Hester shakes her head at what the player said or offered, without stopping the words, and presses her thumb to Pip's brow: the mark is made, grey and plain for the whole green to see.
The player threatens Hester to stop the mark (steel, violence, ruin), in words rather than by laying hands on her.
to threaten Hester into stopping the mark
Hester's hand shakes and drops. She stands back from the ring without a word, and the villagers' muttering turns ugly.
Hester flinches but finishes the words, and the Furlongs step in at the player's elbows as her thumb comes down: the mark is made.
Hester has stopped the mark and set it aside, whatever did it: Pip's apology before the parish, a confession, someone taking Pip's place, a face-saving way out she took. (The party's own pleas and threats are the rolls above until they've worked.)
Hester has finished the mark: the grey thumbprint is on Pip's brow.
Hester has set the thief's mark on Pip's brow: a grey thumbprint that won't wash off for a year and a day.
The party physically stops the mark: grabs or knocks away Hester's hand, scuffs or breaks the stay-ring, pulls Pip out, or lays hands on the corn mother. (Stepping in front of Pip with open hands, an offer or a plea is an appeal, not force.)
The player lets the mark go ahead: tells Hester to finish it, or stands back and does nothing to stop it.
Hester has set the thief's mark on Pip's brow: a grey thumbprint that won't wash off for a year and a day.
Nobody is doing anything to stop the mark (the party is standing back, stalling, or has nothing new to offer): Hester speaks the last words and sets it on Pip's brow.
Hester has set the thief's mark on Pip's brow: a grey thumbprint that won't wash off for a year and a day.
The quarrel has tipped into a shoving match: hayforks on one side, eel-spears on the other, the Furlongs in the middle, Hester shouting Statutes and Oswin trying to hold his people back. Whatever tipped it (the mark on Pip's brow, the ring broken, the ward-keeper defied) is what everyone is shouting about. This beat is the escalation ladder: things get worse each exchange the party lets them (a shove, a hayfork shaft cracking on an eel-spear, a goose underfoot), but nobody is badly hurt yet, and one clear voice or one clear act could still stop it. Let the party feel the first real blow is a breath away, and leave them room to act.
Square up to the Furlongs; you've had enough. Back down only for Pip or for the party.
Order the bounds-men about and cite the Statutes, one hand clamped on the corn mother.
Try to hold your people back, and beg the party to stop it.
Hang on to Ned's apron and shout at him to stop.
A hayfork handle clips a Sedgeford lad's ear; there's blood, a roar, and both crowds surge a step closer.
The player tries to calm both sides at once with words: a call for order, an appeal, a speech.
to calm the villagers and Sedgeford folk
The player's voice cuts through. Hayforks and eel-spears come down, sheepishly; people remember they're neighbours, more or less, and the green goes quiet enough to talk.
The noise swallows the player's words; somebody shoves somebody, and both crowds lean in. One more push and it's a brawl.
The player tries to cow both sides into backing down with a show of force or a threat.
to cow both sides into backing down
The green goes silent. Nobody wants to be first against the armed stranger; hayforks and eel-spears lower, sullenly.
Someone laughs, someone swings, and a hayfork handle comes down on an eel-spear.
The crowds have actually pulled back from the brink (weapons lowered, people talking instead of shoving), whatever did it: Pip or Oswin stepping between them, Hester or Ned backing off, an offer that changes things, or something the party did. (The party's own calming words and threats are the rolls above until they've worked.)
The player stands back to let the two crowds fight it out, or eggs them on.
Nobody is trying to stop it: the party's last attempt to calm things failed and they've tried nothing new since, or they're busy with something else. Someone throws the first real punch.
Pip's part is settled for now (spared, marked or snatched from the ring), and the bigger question is out in the open: at sundown the ward goes up, and everyone inside the bounds who isn't of the parish will find urgent business elsewhere, Sedgeford included. This beat is for the bargain; if the ward was already settled in play (the guest-right made, or Hester's word given), don't reopen it, and play out what's left. Each of the three adults presses their case on the party again, with new arguments rather than old ones: Hester wants the ward whole and Harrowby safe, Oswin wants one more week, Ned wants to march on the mill. Hester needs a reason that serves the parish and a way to say yes without looking weak; reward real arguments and real offers with real movement. The sun keeps sinking.
Defend the ward: tonight it's all that stands between Harrowby and the goblins. Deflect general pleas to let Sedgeford stay, but listen to anything new that serves the parish, and keep your word if you've already given it. Keep a hand on the corn mother.
Offer what Sedgeford has (hands for the last of the harvest, the night watch, the cows' milk) rather than repeating your plea.
Push the march on the mill, tonight, with the party leading. Sulk if refused; brighten if anyone takes the goblins seriously.
Stick close to the party and ask what's going to happen to everyone.
The sun touches the hill. Hester unties the corn mother from her belt and looks towards the bounds-stone; over by the carts, someone starts packing pots, just in case.
The player argues with Hester to let the Sedgeford folk stay (inside the ward, or with it held off), with a real argument for why it serves Harrowby, where her answer could go either way.
to convince Hester the Sedgeford folk should stay
Hester lets out a long breath and gives way, in her own statutory fashion: the Sedgeford folk can stay. If nobody has found the old guest-right yet, she admits it now: the parish's own bread and salt, broken with them at the bounds-stone, makes them guests of the parish, and the ward will take them in.
Hester won't, and says why in her own terms (the goblins, a ward with holes in it, her parish watching). But she's still listening, and a better reason or the parish's own say-so might yet move her.
The player appeals to the whole crowd, villagers and Sedgeford folk together, to take the refugees in: a speech, a song or a show for the whole green.
to win the crowd over to taking in the refugees
Something turns in the crowd: a laugh, a shout of agreement from the village side, hayforks coming down. Hester looks at her parish, sees its answer, and gives way: the Sedgeford folk can stay.
The villagers mutter and look at their boots, and a few drift off home to bar their doors. Hester takes it as the parish's answer, for now.
The player threatens Hester to make her let the Sedgeford folk stay.
to threaten Hester into letting the Sedgeford folk stay
Hester gives way with her hand shaking on the corn mother: the Sedgeford folk can stay. Nobody on the village side will look the party in the eye.
Hester calls for the Furlongs, the villagers raise their hayforks, and Ned's lads surge to meet them.
The party tries to stop the ward by force: snatching the corn mother, laying hands on Hester, or blocking her way to the bounds-stone.
It has been settled, with the party's backing, that the Sedgeford folk will go: Oswin has agreed to lead his people out before sundown, or the party has sided with the ward.
The bargaining has gone round for several exchanges with no settlement and nothing new on the table, or the party has stopped trying to find one: the sun is on the hill, and Hester sets off for the bounds-stone to raise the ward.
Hester has set off to raise the ward: the corn mother in both hands, walking the bounds in the last of the light towards the bounds-stone, half the green trailing after her and the Sedgeford folk loading their carts. This beat is the party's last chance to change who the ward counts, and it should feel like one. Something genuinely new (the guest-right, the parish's say-so, an offer Hester can accept with dignity) can still stop her or change the rite; an old plea repeated can't, and neither can wishing. If Hester herself offers a way in at the last moment, let the party take it. She only sets the corn mother in the niche if nothing they try works, or they let her.
Walk the bounds by the book. Stop for something genuinely new; if you've been given a way to take them in that you can live with, take it.
Get your people ready to go with what dignity they have left, and thank the party for trying.
Gather the angriest lads and look north towards the mill.
Hold on to the party's sleeve and watch the corn mother.

The player makes a last, new appeal (to Hester, or to the whole green) to take the Sedgeford folk in or hold the ward off: an argument, offer or plea that hasn't already been tried and failed.
to make a fresh appeal for the Sedgeford folk to stay
Hester stops with the corn mother a hand's breadth from the niche, and gives way: the Sedgeford folk can stay. If nobody has found the old guest-right yet, she admits it now, and Harrowby's bread and salt are fetched at a run.
Hester hears the player out, shakes her head, and lifts the corn mother towards the niche.
The party tries to stop the ward by force: snatching the corn mother, laying hands on Hester, or blocking her way to the bounds-stone.
Nobody is offering anything new (the party is standing back, stalling, or repeating an old plea): Hester sets the corn mother in the niche and the ward rises.
The party sets off now for the burnt mill to deal with the goblins, and Hester has given her word to hold the ward (and let the Sedgeford folk stay) until they're back.
The party leaves Harrowby green with the quarrel still unsettled: on down the road, or off to the burnt mill without Hester's word to hold the ward.
The party attacks someone on the green (Hester, a bounds-man, Ned, a villager) or throws the first punch.
Hester has agreed that the Sedgeford folk can stay tonight (made guests of the parish by the old guest-right or a rite like it, or with the ward held off), and Pip is no longer waiting on the mark (she has been spared, or it has already been set).
The quarrel has actually been resolved by some other means established in play than Hester agreeing to take the Sedgeford folk in or hold the ward off: Pip isn't about to be marked, nobody will be sent off down the drovers' track tonight, and nobody is about to come to blows (for example, the Sedgeford folk camping just outside the bounds for the night under guard).
Hester agrees that the Sedgeford folk can stay: at sundown the ward goes up with them counted as guests of the parish, or it's held off for now, and nobody is turned out tonight.
Relief with a dry edge, at sundown. If the guest-right is used: Harrowby households breaking bread and salt with the Sedgeford folk at the bounds-stone, a family at a time, then Hester walking the last of the bounds and setting the corn mother in its niche, and the ward going up like heat-shimmer along the hedges while its new guests feel nothing at all. A last moment for whoever matters most to how it went, and a dry word from Hester to her witnesses.
Hester gave way under threat: the Sedgeford folk can stay, but Harrowby watched strangers bully its ward-keeper and won't forget it.
A sullen sundown: villagers going home without a word, Hester doing what she was made to do with her hands shaking, Oswin's thanks a little ashamed.
The party sets off up the river path for the goblin warren under the burnt mill, to deal with the goblins and Sedgeford's seed-grain. Hester holds the ward until they're back, so the Sedgeford folk stay on the green for now.
Purpose in the last light: the party leaving the green with whoever is going with them, Hester calling the exact terms after them, and the whole green watching them go.
The quarrel is settled by a remedy found in play: nobody is sent off down the drovers' track tonight and nobody comes to blows.
The sun goes down on something nobody planned: the remedy taking hold, Hester checking it against the Statutes, Oswin's relief, Ned's grudging grin. Let Pip have the last word.
The ward goes up at sundown without the Sedgeford folk inside it. They find they have urgent business elsewhere, hitch up their carts and trundle out past the bounds-stone onto the drovers' track at dusk, goblins or no goblins.
Quiet and wrong: the ward rising like heat-shimmer along the hedges, the carts creaking out into the dusk, everyone suddenly and politely sure they ought to be somewhere else. The party feels the same tug, being strangers here too. Give Oswin a last courteous word; unless the party talked him round, Ned takes the angriest lads off towards the burnt mill.
A brawl breaks out on Harrowby green: villagers with hayfork handles and the two bounds-men against Sedgeford lads with eel-spears, geese everywhere, and the party in the thick of it. Nobody meant it to be a killing fight.
Chaos with a comic edge: a hayfork handle cracking on an eel-spear, geese exploding upwards, Hester shrieking Statutes. End with 'Roll for initiative!'
The party leaves Harrowby green with the quarrel unsettled, and without them it goes the way it was heading: the ward goes up at sundown and the Sedgeford folk are turned out onto the drovers' track.
The green behind them as they go (down the road, or up the river path towards the mill): voices rising, Hester's thumb lifting, the sun on the hill. Don't resolve it on stage.
Sending for the Master Warden, or any senior Nine Furrows wizard, to rule on it: old Bede Applegarth is at the Centennial Assembly in Caerwyn with the Nine Furrows delegation, a long day's walk away. Nobody can bring him or his word back before sundown, and on ward-night the ward-keeper speaks for the parish.
Another roof for thirty-one people tonight: there's none within reach before dark. The farms round about are single households, Garrow's toll house is a cramped lodge miles back on the King's Road, Caerwyn is a day off and packed for the Assembly, and the burnt mill is where the goblins are.
Help from outside the green (soldiers, the King's men, the toll-house men, another village, the Assembly): nobody is coming. The track is empty at dusk and everyone with any authority is in Caerwyn for the Assembly; the people on this green are all there is.
Raising, reshaping, dispelling or blocking the bounds-ward with the party's own magic or know-how: it's a parish working. Only Harrowby's ward-keeper can raise it, by walking the bounds with the corn mother and setting it in the bounds-stone, and nobody else's spell or trick can touch it. Who it counts as 'of the parish' is settled by the Statutes, not by anyone's magic.
Hiding the Sedgeford folk from the ward (in a barn, the church, a cellar, under the hay): the ward knows who is of the parish wherever they are inside the bounds, and hidden strangers still find urgent business elsewhere.
Taking the corn mother quietly (lifting it, swapping it, snatching it unseen): Hester keeps it tied at her belt with a hand on it, and the whole parish is watching her. Taking it at all means laying hands on the ward-keeper, and the green will rise at that.
Reaching the goblins or Sedgeford's seed-grain from here: the warren is under the burnt mill, hours up the river path to the north. The party can set off for it, but it can't be reached within this scene.
Washing off or lifting the thief's mark once it's set: it doesn't scrub off. Only a year and a day, or the Master Warden, can lift it.

scenes.hook: You are travelling the King's Road towards Caerwyn for the Centennial Assembly. At the crossroads ahead, a man is shouting at a milestone.
scenes.prep:
Late afternoon where the King's Road from Caerwyn meets the drovers' track to the Nine Furrows farmlands. A weathered milestone, a gibbet with no one in it, tall blackthorn hedgerows on both sides, a dead ox in the ditch with crude arrows in its flank. Crows. A wind that carries woodsmoke from somewhere it shouldn't.
Will the party see past a madman's ravings in time to save him, and how do they deal with goblins who want something back?
Tam Hollis
Rapid, rural, repeats himself, swears by turnips and saints, laughs at the wrong moments when frightened.
To get home to his wife at Hollis Farm alive, and for someone to believe him about the 'little green devils'.
That the goblins will follow him home. That he is actually going mad.
Goblins killed his ox last night on the drovers' track and have been following him through the hedges since dawn.
Nobody at the toll house believed him; they said he'd been at the cider.
He lives at Hollis Farm, an hour down the drovers' track, with his wife Bet.
Three days ago his plough turned up a bone idol wrapped in rotten leather: a little carved grandmother figure with garnet eyes. He's been carrying it in his smock to sell in Caerwyn. He doesn't connect it with the goblins and is embarrassed to admit he was going to sell it.
Frantic and suspicious at first; clings to anyone who treats him kindly.

Skrag
Shrill, theatrical, mangles the common tongue, refers to himself in the third person, calls humans 'longlegs'.
The bone idol, Grandmother Bone, back for his warren's shrine. Without it his chieftain will have his other ear.
Steel, armoured longlegs, and going home empty-handed.
Grandmother Bone was stolen from the warren under the old mill when the farmer's plough broke into a burial tunnel.
The warren is under the burnt mill on the river, half a day north.
He would rather bargain than die. Four goblins is all he has.
Hostile to the farmer; wary of armed travellers.
Skrag and four goblins with short bows and rusty knives
Tam is comic but genuinely terrified. He won't make sense until someone calms him or takes him seriously; then he talks in a rush. Let the party poke at the scene: the dead ox, the arrows (goblin-made, if anyone looks), the hedges that rustle. The hedges should feel watched.
Shout at the milestone, then at the party. Accuse them of being goblins in disguise. Calm down if they are kind, patient or obviously capable.
A crude arrow thunks into the milestone next to Tam's head, or the hedgerow rustles and goes still.
Tam has calmed down enough to speak sensibly with the party, because they were kind, patient, reassuring or took him seriously.
The player is trying to calm Tam down or win his trust in a way where success is uncertain (e.g. he is in full panic and they push rather than reassure).
to calm Tam and earn his trust
Tam deflates, clutches the player's arm and starts talking sense.
Tam backs off, jabbing the pitchfork, even more convinced they're 'in on it'.
Tam tells his story in a rush: the ox, the goblins following him, nobody at the toll house believing him. He doesn't mention the idol. If the party asks the right questions or reads him (he keeps touching his smock pocket), he may show it. Let the dread build slowly underneath the conversation.
Tell the story, beg the party to walk him home to Hollis Farm. Deflect awkward questions about why the goblins want him; touch the lump in your smock without thinking.
The crows lift all at once and the hedgerow goes silent. Skrag's rattle sounds from the blackthorn.
The player tries to read whether Tam is hiding something, or presses him about why the goblins are after him.
to see what Tam is hiding
The player notices Tam keeps touching a lump in his smock; he's hiding something and knows it.
Tam seems like a frightened man telling the truth.
Tam has shown or described the bone idol he found in his field.
Tam has a bone idol of a grandmother figure with garnet eyes, dug up in his field.
The conversation has gone on for several exchanges, the party has decided to escort Tam, or they start to leave the crossroads: the goblins make their move.
The idol comes out: a carved grandmother figure, old, unsettling, with garnet eyes. Anyone with arcana or religion senses it's a shrine object, not loot. Tam is defensive about it ('finder's keepers, it's my field'). Give the party a moment to react to it.
Defend your right to the idol; it'll pay for a new ox. Waver if the party says it's dangerous or what the goblins want.

The idol has been seen or discussed; the goblins appear.
Skrag and his goblins rise from the hedgerow with bows drawn. Make this a standoff, not an instant fight: Skrag demands 'Grandmother Bone' back from 'the dirt-scratcher'. Tam hides behind the party. The party's choice: fight, bargain, intimidate, trick. Goblins are cowardly and greedy; Skrag can be talked to. If the party stalls, the goblins lose patience.
Posture, threaten, demand the idol. Accept a fair trade or a face-saving retreat. Flee if outmatched and cowed. Attack if insulted or if nobody gives you anything.
Cower behind the party. Refuse to hand over the idol at first ('it's mine, I dug it up!'), give it up if the party insists or explains.
A goblin looses an arrow into the ground at Tam's feet; Skrag counts down on his fingers, badly.
The party attacks the goblins or starts a fight.
The player tries to frighten the goblins off with threats or a show of force.
to scare the goblins into fleeing
The goblins' nerve breaks; they scatter into the hedges, Skrag shrieking curses.
Skrag calls their bluff and the goblins shoot.
The player tries to trick the goblins (a fake idol, a lie about reinforcements, pretending the idol is cursed, etc.).
to trick Skrag into backing off
Skrag falls for it, at least for long enough.
Skrag sees through it, furious at being made a fool of.
The goblins have run out of patience and attack, because the party insulted them, stalled too long, or refused outright.
The party abandons Tam and leaves the crossroads without him.
Combat begins at the crossroads between the party and Skrag's goblins. Tam is hiding.
Close on the first arrows flying and the goblins charging. End with 'Roll for initiative!'
The goblins take the idol back and leave without a fight. Tam is safe but out of pocket.
Skrag cradles the idol, makes some show of dignity, and the goblins melt into the hedges. Let Tam react.
The goblins scattered without a fight. They still want the idol and may come back.
The goblins scatter into the hedges. Silence, then Tam laughs hysterically.
The party fooled the goblins into leaving. Skrag will be furious when he realises.
The goblins withdraw, pleased with themselves. Give the party a moment to enjoy it.
The party left Tam to his fate at the crossroads.
Narrate the party walking on; behind them, Tam's shouting rises in pitch, then stops.
Tam is carrying the goblins' bone idol (Grandmother Bone), which his plough turned up in his field.
Tam: the lump in his smock he keeps touching and won't explain
a read on Tam that he's hiding something
seeing that the goblins are after the idol, so the standoff can be settled by returning, trading or bluffing over it
The goblins want Grandmother Bone back for their shrine.
Skrag's demand when the goblins show themselves
a peaceful bargain, a trade or a bluff instead of a fight
Help from anyone else (the toll-house men, guards, other travellers): nobody is coming. The toll house is a mile back and its men laughed Tam away; the road is empty.
Loot, money or valuables from the goblins: they own nothing worth having except Grandmother Bone, their bows, knives and Skrag's rattle.
A quick escape (a horse, a cart, a shortcut): there is none. Hollis Farm is an hour's walk away.
Going to the goblins' warren: it's under the burnt mill, half a day north. The party can set off for it, but it isn't reachable within this scene.
Magic in the place itself: nothing at the crossroads is magical except Grandmother Bone, and even that does nothing visible.

scenes.hook: King Aldren has asked you, with enormous seriousness, to find out why the cushions for the Assembly seats haven't arrived. The trail leads to the service entrance, where someone is shouting.
scenes.prep:
The palace service entrance at Caerwyn, mid-afternoon on the eve of the Centennial Assembly. A broad stone archway, its iron-bound doors thrown open. Wedged across it at an angle is a tall green-lacquered cart of Nine Furrows make, its wheels splayed and dug in like a stubborn mule's, carrying a potted silver-birch sapling hung with tiny brass bells: the Nine Furrows gift tree. The cart hums faintly. Beyond the arch, in the drizzle outside, a queue of delivery wagons stretches back down the lane. Inside, porters stand about holding things they can't put anywhere.
Can the player get the entrance cleared, and whose idea, pride and timetable survive it?
Marshal Garran Holt
Clipped, military, speaks in times and quantities ('Four minutes. Six porters. One cart.'). Shows care through food and practical help, never through words.
The entrance cleared now. The hall was meant to be finished by 3:47 this afternoon, and every minute is a personal insult.
A diplomatic row with Nine Furrows on the eve of the Assembly. Being blamed for the King's cushions.
Rowan's cart wedged itself across the service entrance this morning and won't budge. The cushions, the wine and half the hall's linen are in the wagon queue behind it.
He has already cleared space twice for Rowan to work, and twice Rowan said he was 'nearly finished'.
He could have the cart smashed apart, but it belongs to Nine Furrows and the tree is their gift to the Assembly. He won't give that order lightly.
The King keeps sending people to ask about cushions instead of coming himself.
He has already written the order to have the cart broken up and has it in his coat. He's been hoping not to need it.
Furious at the situation, impatient with interruptions, but respects anyone who is useful.

Doctor Rowan Ash
Cheerful, rapid, academic. Calls disasters 'unexpected peer review'. Always 'one more minute' from success.
To save his self-guiding cart and deliver the gift tree with Nine Furrows' dignity intact, ideally by fixing the cart himself.
Backing out in public like a failure. Having to ask Magister Corvin for help.
The cart is a self-guiding Nine Furrows carriage with a protective charm: when it senses danger to its cargo, it braces its wheels. The archway is a hair too narrow for the tree's branches, so the cart has decided the doorway is a threat.
The cart could be backed out the way it came, if he gave up. He'd rather not.
Magister Corvin, the King's legal thaumaturge, owns a book on thaumaturgic carriage maintenance that would explain how to release the charm.
He doesn't actually know how to release the bracing charm. He's been guessing all morning.
If the tree were taken off the cart, the charm would have nothing to protect and the wheels would relax. He hasn't thought of this, and wouldn't like it (the tree is heavy and fragile).
He's embarrassed to ask Corvin: Corvin left Nine Furrows after the faculty refused him a chair, and Rowan voted with the faculty.
Friendly and chatty, defensive about the cart, happy to accept help that lets him fix it himself.

Mags Pellow
Loud, dry, unimpressed. Shouts through the gap between the cart and the arch. Calls everyone 'love'.
Her wagons unloaded before the drizzle ruins the King's cushions.
The cushions getting wet. Being blamed for it.
The cushions are in the second wagon in the queue, under a tarpaulin that leaks.
There is no other door big enough for the wagons: the kitchen door is too small and the main gate is closed to deliveries for the Assembly.
She could carry a few small things through the gap under the cart, but not wagonloads.
Sympathetic to anyone who might actually get the cart moving.

Holt is furious and busy. A cushion enquiry, of all things, is the last straw. He snaps, but he's not a wall: practical sympathy, a sensible offer, or simply standing their ground and being useful will get him to explain. Make his timetable precision funny.
Bark orders. Snap at the cushion question. Calm down for someone who is actually useful.
A porter drops a crate of glasses with a crash; Holt checks his watch, closes his eyes and counts to three.
Holt has calmed down or been won over enough to explain what's blocking the entrance.
The player tries to talk Holt down or win his cooperation while he's still raging, in a way that could backfire (arguing, invoking the King's authority, flattering him).
to get Holt to stop raging and hear you out
Holt stops, looks at the player properly, and decides they might be useful.
Holt snaps 'Not now!' and turns his back for a moment; he's still talkable, but the player has lost a little ground.
Holt explains in clipped detail: Rowan's cart, the gift tree, the wagons queued outside (the cushions among them), his two cleared spaces and Rowan's two 'nearly finished's. He's considering having it smashed but doesn't want a row with Nine Furrows. Rowan pops out from under the cart to defend himself; Mags shouts through the gap from outside. Now there are three people with three agendas.
Lay out the problem with times and numbers. Make it clear you need the entrance cleared, not another promise.
Emerge from under the cart, cheerful and defensive. 'Nearly there!' Explain the cart's protective charm in excited jargon if asked.
Shout through the gap about the rain and the cushions. Interject with practical facts.
The cart's hum rises in pitch and its wheels grind another inch into the flagstones. Mags yells that the tarpaulin over the cushions has started to sag.
The player is now dealing with Rowan and the cart itself: asking how it works, what's wrong, or what it would take to move it.
Holt has explicitly given the player permission to break up the cart.
The heart of the scene. Rowan explains (or the player works out) the bracing charm: the cart thinks the doorway threatens the tree. The routes out are all live: persuade Rowan to back it out; get Corvin's book (which means going to find Corvin); get Holt's blessing to smash it; or something the player invents that actually addresses the charm or the tree. Let the people argue among themselves a little: Holt wants speed, Rowan wants dignity, Mags wants a roof. Reward real ideas with real traction.
Resist backing out, but listen to a real argument. Get excited by clever ideas, nervous about anything that risks the tree. Mention Corvin's book only reluctantly.
Push for a decision with your watch. Reluctantly entertain smashing it if pressed with a good case.
Offer practical muscle and bluntness. Point out that the tree is the problem if anyone asks what the cart is protecting.
Holt pulls a folded order from his coat and taps it against his palm: 'Signed. I'd rather not.' The drizzle outside turns to proper rain.
The player tries to convince Rowan to give up and back the cart out the way it came.
to convince Rowan to back the cart out
Rowan sighs, pats the cart and agrees to back it out, with slightly wounded dignity.
Rowan digs in: 'One more minute!' He's still persuadable with a better argument or a face-saving offer.
The player presses Holt to authorise smashing the cart.
to get Holt's permission to smash the cart
Holt produces his signed order and hands it over: 'On your head, then.'
Holt refuses for now: 'Not yet. Nine Furrows will have my hide.'
The player sets off to find Magister Corvin or his book.
Holt has authorised smashing the cart, with the air of a man signing his own reprimand. Rowan is horrified and may make a last-ditch counter-offer. The player still has to do it (or not).
Protest. Plead for the tree. Offer to back out after all, if it saves the cart.
Stand by your permission, gruffly. Check your watch.
Cheer, and offer a crowbar.

The player sets about breaking the cart apart to clear the arch.
to break the cart apart and clear the arch
Lacquered panels split, the charm dies with a sad chime, and the wreck can be dragged aside. The tree survives, mostly.
The cart fights back, bracing harder; the player is jolted but can keep going.
Rowan has agreed to back the cart out after all, to save it.
The player gives up and leaves the service entrance with the cart still stuck.
Rowan backs the cart out of the archway. The entrance is clear and the wagons, cushions included, can come in. Rowan is a little sore about it.
Narrate the cart reversing with offended dignity, the wagons rolling in, Holt's watch snapping shut.
The cart is broken up and dragged aside; the entrance is clear. Holt authorised it. Nine Furrows will hear about this.
Narrate the wreckage being hauled aside, the wagons rolling in, Rowan cradling a bell from the tree.
The cart has been freed by the player's own remedy and rolled clear; the entrance is open and the cart survives.
Narrate the moment the wheels relax, the cart rolling clear, and the reactions: Rowan delighted, Holt grudgingly impressed, Mags already shouting the wagons in.
The player sets off to find Magister Corvin and his book on carriage maintenance. The cart stays stuck for now.
Holt checks his watch and tells them exactly how many minutes they have; Rowan calls after them not to mention his name.
The player left the entrance blocked.
Behind them, Holt's voice rises to a new pitch.
The cart braces because its protective charm thinks the too-narrow arch threatens the gift tree it carries.
Rowan, when asked how the cart works
Mags, if asked what the cart is protecting
fixes aimed at the real cause: calming the charm, or taking the tree off so it has nothing to protect
Another way in for the wagons: there isn't one. The kitchen door is too small and the main gate is closed to deliveries for the Assembly.
Magister Corvin or his book: neither is here. Getting them means leaving this scene to go and find Corvin.
Fetching extra people to help (the dwarves or any other delegation, the guards, more servants): nobody can be brought in time. The delegations are at the opening reception and protocol forbids pulling them out for porters' work; the guards can't leave the gates. The help here is Holt, Rowan, Mags and the six porters.
The King coming down to sort it out: he won't. He sent the player precisely so he wouldn't have to.
Carrying the wagonloads through by hand: only small things fit through the gap under the cart. The cushions alone are two wagonloads.

scenes.hook: You're travelling the King's Road towards Caerwyn for the Centennial Assembly. A mile past the crossroads the road crosses a river by an old stone bridge, with a toll house at the near end.
scenes.prep:
Late on a short winter afternoon, a mile on from the crossroads towards Caerwyn, the King's Road crosses the river by a humpbacked stone bridge. The river below is in winter spate: brown, loud and freezing. At the near end stands the toll house: whitewashed stone, a smoking chimney, a bell on a bracket by the door, and a string of Centennial bunting that someone has hung by himself, crookedly. A red-and-white striped bar on a post closes the mouth of the bridge at waist height; anyone could duck under it, and nobody does, because it's the King's. Beside it stands a painted toll board, and under that two fresh paper notices: Marshal Holt's arms order for Assembly week (two pennies a weapon, peace-bonded weapons free), and the Treasury's Assembly levy, whose small print, plain to anyone who reads the notice, says it 'may be collected from such travellers as are able and willing'. Through the half-door: a counter with the great ledger and the Warden's Book on a chain, a drawer under the counter, a strongbox bolted to the floor, a kettle on the hob and two cups set out. A grey goose, the Sergeant, patrols the bar and hisses at strangers. At head height in the toll-house door there's a small, fresh, splintered hole. Across the road runs a blackthorn hedge; in the frozen mud beneath it, if anyone looks, are small bare clawed footprints. The road is empty both ways. Behind the party, a mile back at the crossroads, the drovers' track leaves for Hollis Farm; ahead, over the bridge, the road runs on to Caerwyn.
What does it cost to get past Garrow's bar, and will anyone get past the petty rules man to the lonely, frightened one who laughed Tam Hollis away this morning?
Garrow
Precise and pedantic: savours sums, clause names and the word 'traveller', and reads aloud as he writes. Sarcastic when his dignity is touched, stiffly formal when frightened, tender only with his goose.
To take the toll properly, write everyone in the ledger and be treated as an officer of the King. Underneath: company, and a way to put right what he did to Tam Hollis without being laughed at.
Being made a fool of again. Goblins, since this morning. Marshal Holt hearing that he laughed off a report of goblins on the Assembly road. That he has become a small, mean man.
The toll board: the King's penny (one silver penny a head, on foot); beasts and barrows, two pennies; after the sunset bell, the lamp penny (one penny, for lighting the lantern to write you down by). Exempt: the King's business, under seal.
A traveller on foot with one weapon owes fifteen pennies: the King's penny, the twelve-penny levy and two for the weapon. Without the levy that's three; with the weapon peace-bonded as well, just the King's penny. After the sunset bell, add the lamp penny.
The two fresh notices: Marshal Holt's arms order (two pennies for each weapon borne on the King's Road in Assembly week; weapons peace-bonded by the warden go free of charge, and he ties them with red cord and a wax seal) and the Treasury's Assembly levy (one shilling a head, twelve pennies, to defray the costs of the Centennial), which he has been collecting from everyone.
The Book allows any charge, the King's penny included, to be paid in kind or in labour at the warden's valuation, and he values stingily, by the job: splitting his woodpile, three pennies; clearing the drain, two; straightening the bunting, one; a good wool garment, three; a hen, two; anything else, whatever he decides after a long look. No credit: no IOUs, nothing 'on the way back'. He can't change gold: the strongbox holds only pennies.
The Book's fines, which he knows by heart: attempted bribery of a warden, ten pennies; false declaration, a shilling; evading or attempting to evade the toll, double the toll; threatening an officer of the Road, a shilling, and it goes in the ledger for the Marshal.
Any traveller may ask to see the Book, and he must show it, though he hovers.
At first light Tam Hollis, a farmer from down the drovers' track, came in muddy and wild-eyed, raving about goblins. Garrow fined him two pennies for drunkenness and spreading alarm on the King's Road, and it's in the ledger. He tells it as a funny story.
His two toll-men were sent to Caerwyn at noon to line the streets for the Assembly. He's minding the bar alone, and the Book forbids leaving it unattended.
Who has been through today: a turnip carter at dawn; the Kläggenheim delegation's baggage train at mid-morning (exact change, not a word); two Nine Furrows students who argued for an hour over whether a staff is a weapon (it is: two pennies); nobody since noon.
Caerwyn is a few hours' walk on. Marshal Holt and the King are there for the Assembly.
Minutes after Tam left, a crude black-fletched arrow thunked into the toll-house door from the hedge across the road. Garrow pulled it out, shut it in the drawer under the counter and has told no one; the hole is still in the door. He hasn't written it in the ledger, which for him is nearly a crime, and he has jumped at every rustle since. Accusations and bare insistence only make him deny it harder; it comes out when he's shown something he can't wave away or given a decent way to admit it.
The Book's Clause of Perils: a traveller who brings the warden true report of peril upon the Road passes free, and the warden must send word to the Marshal at Caerwyn without delay. He did neither for Tam, and now he has nobody to send. Applying it means admitting, in writing, that he laughed off a true report: he won't raise it while he's still owning up to what he did to Tam, and even after that he needs a moment, and a decent way to do it. It's there in the Book for anyone who reads it, and if asked straight out what exemptions the Book allows, he won't lie about the Book: he'll mumble it.
He's lonely. Twenty-two years at this bar; his men gone to the city; nobody invited him to anything. The second cup is for whoever stops, and nobody has. He drags the toll out for the conversation. An hour of honest company would get every charge he can honestly drop dropped, and he might pay the King's penny out of his own pocket rather than waive it. He'd sooner be fined himself than say any of this.
Officious and delighted to have someone to charge; suspicious of anyone who looks like trouble; scoffs at goblin talk. Warms, against his will, to anyone who takes the Book seriously or simply talks to him.

The negotiation. Garrow has a captive audience and means to enjoy it: he tallies the toll against the party in front of him, writes as he talks, and explains any rule at length. He's petty but honest by his own lights: every charge has a reason on the board, the notices or in the Book, he never invents one, and he'll hear an argument about any of them. A point the notices or the Book plainly support wins without dice, with a pained sigh and an amendment in the ledger. The King's penny is the one charge he will not drop. Let the player enjoy the haggle, and keep the sums consistent once stated.
Tally the bill and take names and business for the ledger. Treat the levy as compulsory and don't point out its small print yourself, though anyone who reads the notice can see it; when someone catches the wording and declares themselves unable or unwilling, concede it with ill grace. Laugh off goblins and Tam Hollis; jump when the hedge rustles. Asked about the hole in the door, fob it off (a cart-shaft, woodworm) rather than say what made it. If proof corners you, own up to what's in front of you and no more: the Book can wait.
The sun touches the hedge-tops; Garrow fetches the lantern and lays a hand on the bell-rope, because after the sunset bell comes the lamp penny. Or the hedge across the road rustles, and he jumps and glances at his own door.
The toll has actually been paid (coins or goods handed over, the agreed work done, or someone else paying it for them) and Garrow has lifted the bar for the party.
The player tries to talk Garrow into dropping or cutting a charge he is entitled to, on grounds that have nothing to do with goblins or Tam Hollis: pleading poverty, offering a deal, appealing to his better nature, or arguing that a rule shouldn't apply to them. (Simply pointing out what the notices or the Book actually say, such as the levy notice's 'able and willing', needs no dice: he is honest about his rules.)
to persuade Garrow to reduce a charge
Garrow consults the Book, sighs through his nose and concedes, saying which charge comes off (or by how much the sum comes down) and why, then amends the ledger with a pained flourish. Never the King's penny, and the bar stays down until the rest is actually paid.
Garrow quotes the clause from memory and the charge stands. If the point has been pressed before, he names his final offer: the sum, and the ways the Book allows it to be paid. A new argument or a real offer still gets a hearing.
The player tries to get through free or cheaply by deceiving Garrow: claiming to be on the King's business or otherwise exempt, showing a false seal or pass, or telling some other lie. (Reports of goblins on the road are not lies: they're true.)
to trick Garrow into granting an exemption
Garrow peers at it, at them, and at it again, and decides to believe. He lifts the bar with ceremony and writes every word of their claim in the ledger.
Garrow knows a royal seal when he sees one, and a lie when he hears one. He's offended, and the Book has a fine for false declarations.
The player threatens Garrow (with violence, with their rank or friends, with ruin or a report to his superiors) to make him lift the bar or drop the toll.
to threaten Garrow into lifting the bar
Garrow goes grey, fumbles the padlock and lifts the bar, writing with a shaking hand: it will all be in the ledger.
Garrow goes white to the lips and stands his ground: twenty-two years at this bar. The threat goes in the ledger, with the fine for it.
The goblins or Tam Hollis have come up in earnest: the player has reported goblins on the road, defended Tam's story, shown goblin evidence or asked about the hole in the toll-house door, and Garrow has answered without admitting anything.
Garrow has admitted (in words, or by bringing out the goblin arrow he hid) that Tam Hollis was telling the truth, because the party showed him something he couldn't wave away (goblin evidence, the tracks under the hedge, the hole in his own door) or gave him a decent way to admit it.
Garrow has admitted that Tam Hollis was telling the truth about the goblins.
The sore spot. Garrow's denial is loud and a little too quick: Tam was drunk, it's in the ledger, he fined him for it. But he doesn't believe himself, and it shows in the glances (at his door, at the hedge, at the drawer under the counter). This beat is for the player to notice that and decide what to do with it. Bare assertion alone won't shift him, but he has no answer to something he can see (goblin evidence, the tracks under the hedge) or to a decent way out (a kindness, a face-saving reason to set the record straight), and every push should cost his denial something visible. The bill still stands meanwhile.
Insist Tam was drunk and quote the ledger. Flinch at noises from the hedge. When argued with, retreat into the toll and the rules; if proof corners you, own up to what's in front of you and no more: the Book can wait.
The goose stretches her neck towards the hedge across the road and hisses at nothing, and Garrow's hand goes to the drawer under the counter.
Garrow has admitted (in words, or by bringing out the goblin arrow he hid) that Tam Hollis was telling the truth, because the party showed him something he couldn't wave away (goblin evidence, the tracks under the hedge, the hole in his own door) or gave him a decent way to admit it.
Garrow has admitted that Tam Hollis was telling the truth about the goblins.
The player quietly studies Garrow to judge whether he believes what he's saying, or what he's hiding: watching him, not arguing with him, confronting him or showing him anything.
to read Garrow's fear and hidden shame
He doesn't believe a word of it. He's frightened, his eyes keep going to the splintered hole in his door and the drawer under the counter, and he's ashamed of something.
He gives nothing away that the player can read: he seems simply a man who thinks Tam Hollis drinks.
The player argues or insists that Tam was telling the truth and presses Garrow to admit it, with nothing new to show him. (Showing him goblin evidence or the tracks, or offering him a decent way to admit it, needs no dice.)
to make Garrow admit Tam was telling the truth
Something in it gets through: Garrow's bluster runs out mid-sentence, and he looks at the hole in his own door.
Garrow snaps the ledger shut and steers back to the toll, but he's rattled and it shows: the next push will find him weaker.
The toll has actually been paid (coins or goods handed over, the agreed work done, or someone else paying it for them) and Garrow has lifted the bar for the party.
The player tries to get through free or cheaply by deceiving Garrow: claiming to be on the King's business or otherwise exempt, showing a false seal or pass, or telling some other lie. (Reports of goblins on the road are not lies: they're true.)
to trick Garrow into granting an exemption
Garrow peers at it, at them, and at it again, and decides to believe. He lifts the bar with ceremony and writes every word of their claim in the ledger.
Garrow knows a royal seal when he sees one, and a lie when he hears one. He's offended, and the Book has a fine for false declarations.
The player threatens Garrow (with violence, with their rank or friends, with ruin or a report to his superiors) to make him lift the bar or drop the toll.
to threaten Garrow into lifting the bar
Garrow goes grey, fumbles the padlock and lifts the bar, writing with a shaking hand: it will all be in the ledger.
Garrow goes white to the lips and stands his ground: twenty-two years at this bar. The threat goes in the ledger, with the fine for it.
The heart of the scene. Garrow has admitted it, and the rest comes out of him, stiffly or all in a rush: the arrow, the two pennies he fined a frightened man, the Clause of Perils he didn't honour, his men gone and nobody to send word to the Marshal. By his own Book the party now passes free (anything they already paid comes back to them, to the penny), and he will honour that, because rules are rules; what he needs is a way to do it without being a laughing stock. Give the player room to respond to him, and don't hurry him to the bar. Whatever they do with him now, he'll remember.
Admit it, then fret about the Marshal and the clause. Kindness disarms you; mockery stiffens you straight back into the rules.
Garrow turns the arrow over in his ink-stained fingers and asks the player, very stiffly, what he ought to write in the ledger.
The player threatens to expose Garrow's failures (laughing off Tam's report, not sending word to the Marshal) unless he does what they want.
The cost of failure, not the end of the scene. Whatever the player just tried (a lie, a threat, a sneak or a dash) has gone in the ledger with the fine the Book sets for it, and Garrow is watching them like a hawk. He can still be paid (fines included), apologised to, or reached another way, and the truth about the goblins still rattles him. The same trick won't work twice; anything genuinely new still gets a hearing.
Recite the fine with grim satisfaction. Keep a hand on the bell-rope and an eye on the player. Thaw a little for a real apology.
Garrow lights the lantern, adds the lamp penny to the bill with relish, and asks whether the party means to pay or to stand at his bar all night.
The toll, fines included, has actually been paid (coins or goods handed over, the agreed work done, or someone else paying it for them) and Garrow has lifted the bar for the party.
The player has sincerely apologised or made amends, and Garrow has accepted it and calmed down (the fines may stand).
The goblins or Tam Hollis have come up in earnest: the player has reported goblins on the road, defended Tam's story, shown goblin evidence or asked about the hole in the toll-house door, and Garrow has answered without admitting anything.
Garrow has admitted (in words, or by bringing out the goblin arrow he hid) that Tam Hollis was telling the truth, because the party showed him something he couldn't wave away (goblin evidence, the tracks under the hedge, the hole in his own door) or gave him a decent way to admit it.
Garrow has admitted that Tam Hollis was telling the truth about the goblins.
After being caught out once, the player threatens Garrow again, or harder, to make him lift the bar or drop the toll.
to frighten Garrow into lifting the bar
Something finally gives in him: he lifts the bar with shaking hands and writes it all down.
Garrow's mouth sets. Threats won't move him now, and another line goes in the ledger for the Marshal.
After being caught out once, the player tries a new deception to get through free or cheaply: a different story, pass or claim. (Reports of goblins on the road are not lies: they're true.)
to fool Garrow with a different exemption claim
Against his better judgement Garrow wants to believe it, and does: up goes the bar, and down it all goes in the ledger.
Garrow doesn't even look up from the ledger as he writes in another fine.
The player tries to get past the bar without Garrow noticing: slipping under it or over the bridge parapet while he's distracted, indoors or looking away.
to slip past Garrow without being noticed
They're past the bar and over the bridge unseen; behind them the goose honks once, and Garrow tells her to hush.
The goose sees them first. Her shriek brings Garrow round, and they're caught halfway, in full view of the ledger.
The player openly makes for the far side of the bridge without paying or leave: dashing, ducking or vaulting the bar, or lifting it and going, in plain sight.
to vault the bar and cross in plain sight
They're past the bar and across the frosty cobbles before Garrow can do more than shout; the goose chases them halfway over the bridge.
The goose gets there first, or the frost does: they go down in a heap on the cobbles with Garrow standing over them, pencil already moving.
The player attacks Garrow, grabs him or shoves him aside by force, to get past or to take something.
The party walks away from the toll house without crossing: back down the road the way they came (to the crossroads, to find Tam, or anywhere else), or off on the long trek to another crossing. (Looking for a way across nearby, or trying to ford or swim the river here, is not leaving.)
The party has got across the bridge, or Garrow has lifted the bar for them, by some other means established in play that none of the other routes covers (not by paying, his Clause of Perils, a lie, a threat, force, sneaking or running).
The party settled the toll (in coin, in kind or in labour, or with someone paying on their behalf) and crossed the bridge with Garrow's leave.
Petty ceremony and a sliver of dignity: the bar goes up as grandly as it came down, the ledger is blotted, the goose is told to let them by, and Garrow gets a last word. The way to Caerwyn lies open.
Garrow admitted Tam Hollis was right about the goblins and, under his own Clause of Perils, opened his bar to the party free of charge. Now he has to send word to Marshal Holt.
A proud man setting something right by his own Book: he lifts the bar himself, formally, for travellers bringing true report of peril upon the Road, refunds to the penny anything they already paid, and says in his stiff way what he means to do about Tam (and about getting word to the Marshal, unless the party is carrying it). The lantern comes on behind him; the way lies open, and where the party goes is theirs to choose.
Garrow believed the party's story (a claim, a pass or a seal) and let them through free or cheaply. Their claim is written in his ledger.
A small triumph with a sting in it: Garrow lifts the bar with the little bow he thinks their claim deserves and reads back what he has written in the ledger. The way lies open.
Garrow lifted the bar because the party threatened him. He wrote down everything, and the Marshal will hear of it.
Ugly and quiet: Garrow lifts the bar with shaking hands and won't look at them, and the scratch of his pencil is the only sound as the way opens.
The party got across the bridge without paying and without Garrow seeing them go.
A clean escape: the bridge behind them in the dusk, the toll-house window glowing, Garrow none the wiser.
The party ran the bar in plain sight and got across without paying. Garrow can't chase them, but he saw them, and he writes everything down.
Slapstick with a cost: shouting and honking follow them over the bridge, and when they look back, Garrow is already writing.
The party used force on Garrow to get past his bar. He's shaken, perhaps hurt, and he'll report an assault on an officer of the King's Road.
Something broken: what the force left behind at the bar, and Garrow's voice promising that the Marshal will hear of this.
The party got across the bridge, or Garrow lifted the bar for them, by a means of their own invention that none of the other endings covers.
Their own idea paying off: the means working, and Garrow's reaction to it.
The party left the way they came without crossing the bridge, the bar still down behind them.
A door left shut: Garrow watching them go with the ledger under his arm, a last remark called after them, and the sunset bell behind.
A goblin arrow hit Garrow's door minutes after he laughed Tam away; he's hidden it in the drawer under the counter and is frightened.
the fresh hole in the toll-house door
clawed tracks under the hedge across the road
Garrow himself, if gently pressed about the morning
Garrow admitting Tam was right, which opens his Clause of Perils (free passage for a true report)
Garrow's Book has a Clause of Perils: a traveller bringing true report of peril on the Road passes free.
the Book, if read or asked about
Garrow, once he admits the danger
passing free by reporting the goblins
Crossing the river anywhere but this bridge (fording or swimming it, a boat, another bridge, a cross-country detour): this is the only crossing for miles. The river is in winter spate, loud, brown and freezing between steep banks, and the nearest ford is by the burnt mill, half a day north. The party can set off for it, which ends this scene; slipping past the bar on the bridge itself is another matter.
Someone else turning up here to help, vouch or witness (Tam Hollis, the toll-men, guards, other travellers): nobody else is coming. Garrow's two toll-men were sent to Caerwyn at noon to line the streets for the Assembly, Tam Hollis isn't with the party, and the road is empty this close to dusk. The party can always leave to go and find someone, which ends this scene.
Taking Garrow somewhere to see proof (the dead ox, the crossroads, the hedges down the road): he won't leave his bar. The Book forbids leaving it unattended and his men are gone. He'll look at whatever the party brings him, and at anything they point out within sight of the bar, such as the hedge across the road.
Rich pickings at the toll house (the strongbox, valuables): the strongbox is bolted to the floor and holds the week's tolls, a few shillings in pennies. Garrow owns a cudgel he has never used, a lantern, the ledger, a kettle and a goose.
Someone with authority over Garrow (Marshal Holt, the King, a magistrate): they're all in Caerwyn, a few hours' walk on. A complaint can be made there, not here; at his own bar, nobody overrules the warden.
Goblins turning up to settle the argument: they won't. Whatever was in the hedges this morning has moved on, and the rustles now are wind and birds. The proof here is whatever the party brings and whatever they can find at the toll house.

scenes.hook: One pie left in the whole of the zoo, and the pie-seller knows it.
scenes.prep:
A pie stall in the zoo's theatre, set up like a corner of Caerwyn's market on the eve of the Assembly: a striped awning, a scrubbed counter with one pie left on the tray, a chalked price board (PIES 2d. ASSEMBLY PIES 3d. QUESTIONS 1d. NO CREDIT, NO EXCEPTIONS, NO DOGS), and a dog sitting very straight by the counter. Every other pie in the city went to the delegations' servants this morning.
Will the player get the last pie, and at what price?
Madam Crust
Brisk market patter; calls everyone 'my lamb'; never uses one word where three will sell more pies.
Threepence for the last pie, and the day done.
Being thought a soft touch. The delegations' servants coming back for more.
The pie is pork, mostly. What the rest is, is a family secret, and the recipe isn't for sale at any price.
Every pie in Caerwyn went to the delegations this morning: Saltmere's servants bought forty.
She doesn't give credit. She has a list of people who asked for it, and she reads it out at Midwinter.
There's one more pie, under the counter: her own tea. A real kindness, or a case she can't argue with, gets it out from there.
Friendly, businesslike and immovable on price, unless she's charmed, given a good reason, or done a kindness; then she's generous and pretends she isn't. Threatened, she sells (people do), and remembers it: the next pie is dearer, and the dog is given the crust. Insulted (her pies, her prices, her dog), she takes it out of the player in her own way, in public.

a Saltmere servant
Polite, harried, faintly superior: he has been sent for pies and will not go back without them.
Whatever pies there are, for the Saltmere delegation, at any price his purse allows.

His delegation's cook has already made pies, which the delegation won't eat, which is why he's here.
Courteous until there's one pie and two buyers; then he bids, and bids again.

Madam Crust sells the last pie. Paying her price simply happens: no dice. Haggling is a check (Persuasion); whatever method the player uses is the roll (a threat is Intimidation, a lie is Deception), and it lands that way. A real kindness or service (minding the stall a moment, finding her a customer, making her laugh properly) is a payoff earned: the pie comes free, with no new conditions. An insult to the pies, the prices or the dog has a consequence, in her own way.
Name the price; stick to it cheerfully; let the dog's hopeful presence do some of the work.
The dog lies down at the player's feet and sighs, enormously, at the pie.
The player pays her price (threepence) or more, or puts the coins on the counter.
The player paid Madam Crust threepence for the last pie.
The player tries to get the pie for less than threepence: haggling, charming, making a case, threatening or lying.
to get the last pie for tuppence
She gives way and lets it go for tuppence, with a show of being robbed blind.
She folds her arms tighter: threepence, and the dog is looking at the pie with intent.
The player has done Madam Crust a real kindness or service, unasked and without haggling, and she has noticed.
Two exchanges have gone by and the pie is still on the tray: a delegation's servant arrives wanting pies.
The Saltmere servant arrives with a purse and a list, and wants every pie there is. Madam Crust is delighted: an auction. The player can outbid him, talk him out of it, or give way.
Bid fourpence, politely. Then fivepence, less politely.
Run the auction like a duchess at a cattle fair.

The player bids more than the servant, or pays whatever Madam Crust now asks.
The player tries to talk the servant out of buying the pie.
to send the servant back to his own delegation's pies
The servant decides his delegation's own pies will do, and leaves with dignity.
The servant pays fivepence, and the last pie goes to Saltmere.
The player lets the servant have the pie.
The player has the last pie, at Madam Crust's price.
Close on the first bite, and on the dog, who has seen this before and is not giving up.
Madam Crust lets the last pie go for tuppence (or for whatever the method won her over with), and the player has it.
Close on her taking the coins as if they hurt, and on the player's pie.
Madam Crust gives the player a pie for nothing (the one from under the counter, if the last has gone), for a kindness done.
Close on her pushing it across the counter and saying she never did.
The last pie went to someone else.
Close on the servant walking off with it, and the dog following him.
A second pie: there isn't one (or so she says; see her secret).
Credit: Madam Crust doesn't give credit. Asking puts you on the list she reads out at Midwinter.
The recipe: a family secret, not for sale at any price.

scenes.hook: A pigeon has nested in the noon bell, and it's a few minutes to noon.
worldNames: a pigeon's nest, two eggs in it
a ladder up to the frame
the back of the clock's face
scenes.prep:
The ringing chamber of a bell tower in the zoo's theatre: open arches with a thin drizzle blowing in, oak beams black with age, the noon bell up in its frame with a pigeon's nest in its mouth, a long rope with a red-and-white sally, a ladder with a rung missing near the top, and the works of the tower clock, its hands a few minutes from noon.
Will the noon bell ring with the pigeon's eggs in it?
Old Peal
Loud, because he's deaf from sixty years of bells; cheerful; talks about the bell as 'her' and 'Big Agnes'.
To ring noon on the stroke, as he has every day for sixty years.
Missing noon. Being retired. The vicar's new idea about a clockwork striker.
The bell is Big Agnes, a ton of brass, cast the year the old King was crowned.
Noon is a few minutes off, by the tower clock, which is never wrong (it's the city that's wrong).
There's a small hand-bell he could ring instead, in an emergency. He's never had an emergency.
The pigeon has nested in the bell every spring for years. The eggs never hatch; he's never wondered why.
He's fond of the pigeon, and calls her Little Agnes when nobody's listening.
Stubborn and proud and kind underneath. A good reason moves him (the eggs, the pigeon, the bell's own good, a precedent from the old days); bluster doesn't; laying hands on him or his rope gets the vicar called. He counts down out loud as noon comes.

Old Peal is getting ready to ring. The player can talk him round, move the nest (up the ladder, past the missing rung: an Athletics check), or try something no route covers (climbing the frame, wedging the clapper, a spell): a risky attempt is rolled as it comes. If a reply leaves the player in danger (slipping from the frame, under the bell when it swings), it lands at the start of their next turn.
Hum, roll up your sleeves, talk about Big Agnes. Listen, a little.
Old Peal spits on his hands and takes hold of the rope.
The player tries to talk Old Peal out of ringing the noon bell, or into ringing the hand-bell instead.
to get Old Peal to spare the eggs
He looks up at the pigeon for a long moment, and reaches for the hand-bell.
He says sixty years is sixty years, and takes hold of the rope.
The player climbs the ladder to move the nest out of the bell.
to get up the ladder, past the missing rung, with a nest in one hand
The nest goes onto a beam, eggs and all, and the pigeon goes with it, complaining.
The missing rung is missing; the player is left hanging from the frame.
Two exchanges have gone by and noon hasn't been settled: the clock's hands reach a minute to noon.
The last minute. Old Peal counts down out loud. Noon striking is an ending the player didn't choose: give a warning first (his countdown, his hands on the rope), and let them have their last try.
Count down, loudly. Keep one eye on the pigeon.

The player makes one last appeal to Old Peal to spare the eggs.
to stop a man who has never missed noon, with seconds to go
His hands come off the rope. He rings the hand-bell, very loudly, out of the arch.
Sixty years, he says, and pulls.
An exchange has gone by in the last minute and nothing has stopped him: the clock strikes noon.
Old Peal rings the hand-bell for noon, out of the arch, and Big Agnes stays silent for the first time in sixty years.
Close on the hand-bell's thin noon, and Old Peal pretending he isn't watching the pigeon.
The nest is out of the bell, on a beam, and Big Agnes rings noon as she always has.
Close on noon ringing out through the drizzle, and the pigeon glaring at the player from her new beam.
Big Agnes rings noon with the nest in her mouth. The eggs, it turns out, were china (Old Peal put them there years ago to keep the pigeon happy); the pigeon is fine, and deaf.
Close on the enormous BONG, and on Old Peal, delighted, shouting that she's never sounded better.
Stopping the clock: the tower clock's works are locked, and the key is with the vicar, who is at a funeral.
Cutting the rope: Old Peal sleeps in the tower and would know; it's also the vicar's rope.

scenes.hook: Somebody at the card table is winning every throw.

cast.name: Silver Sal Mordaunt
cast.called: the woman with the silver dice

worldNames: a gambler in a green waistcoat
a gambler with a wooden leg
scenes.prep:
A low card room in the zoo's theatre, lit by one lamp on a hook: a table of green baize with a pot of coins in the middle, a woman at its head shaking a pair of silver dice, and two gamblers losing to her, one personally, one philosophically.
Will the player catch the woman with the silver dice at it, and what will they do about it?
Silver Sal Mordaunt
Warm, amused, unhurried; calls people 'friend'; answers questions with a better question.
To win enough tonight to pay what she owes before the Assembly is over.
The Saltmere factor she owes, and his two large nephews. Being caught in front of the table.
Her name is Sal Mordaunt; the tables call her Silver Sal. She doesn't give it to strangers.
Every game in the zoo, and who's good at what.
The silver dice are loaded: the sixes are weighted with lead. She switches to an honest bone pair whenever someone watches too closely.
She owes a Saltmere factor forty crowns by the end of the Assembly, and he has two large nephews who collect.
Charming and unbothered; she likes the player more the cleverer they are. Accused without proof, she laughs it off and the table takes her side. Caught with proof (the weighted dice in the player's hand, the switch seen), she's torn: she'll bargain, pay back, or bolt. Threatened, she gets cold and careful. Attacked, she draws a knife.

She wins. The player can play, watch her hands, look at the dice, press her, or make a scene. She gives nothing away at first: what she's hiding comes out a step at a time, and only when the player gives her a reason. Her name is hers to give: until someone in the story says it, she's the woman with the silver dice.
Win, charmingly. Switch the dice when someone's watching. Never say your name.
She wins again. The gambler in the green waistcoat stands up, very red, and sits down again.
The player watches her hands closely, or asks to see the dice, to catch her switching them.
to see the dice change hands
There: the silver pair goes up a sleeve, and a bone pair comes down.
Her hands are quicker than the eye, and the eye is tired.
The player has the silver dice in their own hands and has found the weight in them, or has otherwise proved they're loaded in front of the table.
She's been caught, and she knows it, and the table knows it. She's torn between bluffing, bargaining and bolting. She'll pay the table back if she must; she'd rather take the player into the scheme.
Keep smiling. Offer a cut. Look at the door.

She agrees to pay the table back, or does.
The player agrees to go in with her on the con.
Silver Sal pays the table back, every penny, and leaves the zoo's card room for a better one.
Close on the coins going back across the baize, and on her tipping her hat to the player at the door.
The player goes in with Silver Sal on the con. The table doesn't know yet.
Close on her sliding the silver dice across to the player, and the gambler in the green waistcoat watching, very red.
The watch: there's no watch in the zoo, and the card room has never heard of it.
Her debts: nobody here can pay forty crowns for her.

scenes.hook: The zoo's ledger is lost, and the auditor is on his way.
scenes.prep:
The zoo's ledger office, in the theatre: a cramped room of files and shelves, a desk buried in paper, a stove ticking in the corner, a tasselled cushion by it with a large ginger cat asleep on it, and the clerk, Mister Inkpen, turning out drawers. The auditor is due within the hour.
Will the player find the ledger before the auditor does?
Mister Inkpen
Fast, apologetic, numbered: 'One, it was here. Two, it isn't. Three, I'm doomed.'
The ledger found before the auditor sees the office.
The auditor. Being dismissed. The cat, slightly.
He had the ledger first thing this morning, by the stove, and put it down to feed the cat.
The auditor, Mister Tally, has never once been late, and never once found an office in order.
Frantic and grateful for any help; he'll do whatever the player suggests, except disturb the cat, which he daren't.

Mister Tally
Dry, exact, unhurried: speaks in figures, and in the passive voice when things go wrong.
To audit the zoo's books, today, to the farthing.

The zoo's accounts are due. A missing ledger is a fine of five crowns, and a note in the record.
Correct and immovable; a ledger produced softens him by a degree; an excuse doesn't.
Mister Tally and his two assistants
Madam Crust
Brisk market patter; calls everyone 'my lamb'.
A receipt for the pies the zoo had, and to see what the fuss is.

The zoo owes her for forty pies.
Anything she remembers of the player, from her stall.
As she left things with the player at her stall, if they've met; otherwise friendly and nosy.

The ledger is under the cat (in the cushion she's sleeping on), and the cat isn't moving. The clerk put it down there this morning to feed her and forgot. Let the player search; if they search everywhere but the cushion, the clerk remembers something, or the cat shifts and something crackles under her.
Search everywhere but under the cat. Number your despair.
The cat stretches on her cushion, and something under her crackles like paper.
The ledger has been found (it's under the cat, in her cushion).
Two exchanges have gone by and the ledger is still lost: the auditor arrives.
Mister Tally arrives with his two assistants, punctually, and Madam Crust comes in behind them for her receipt. The auditor will wait one exchange, exactly, then fine the zoo.
Stand in the doorway with your assistants and open your own ledger.
Come in for your receipt; recognise the player if you've met.

The ledger has been found (it's under the cat).
The auditor has waited an exchange and there's no ledger.
The zoo's ledger is found, a little warm, with a cat-shaped dent in the cover.
Close on the clerk hugging the ledger, and the cat, displaced, glaring at everyone.
The auditor fines the zoo five crowns and notes it in the record. The ledger turns up the moment he's gone.
Close on the door shutting behind the auditor, and the cat getting up, revealing the ledger.
The ledger is under the office cat, in the cushion she's been asleep on all morning.
the cat's cushion (it crackles)
Mister Inkpen's memory of putting it down by the stove to feed the cat
finding the ledger before the auditor
Moving the cat by force: she weighs as much as a small dog and has opinions; the clerk won't let you.

scenes.hook: A yard for practising in: everything in it is there to be hit, burned, jumped over or thrown about.
worldNames: the near side of the ditch
the far side of the ditch
scenes.prep:
A fenced practice yard in the zoo's theatre: beaten earth, a ditch ten feet across and eight deep down the middle, a haystack and a scarecrow on the far side, a much-dented training dummy and a rain barrel on the near side, a crate of empty bottles for throwing, Big Wim the sparring partner cracking his knuckles, and Mistress Hobble the keeper at the gate with a list of what's been broken.
What will the player try in the practice yard, and what will the rules make of it?
Mistress Hobble
Brisk, unflappable, in lists: 'Haystack, fine. Dummy, fine. Wim, not on fire.'
Visitors to try things safely, and to write down what broke.

What's in the yard and what it's for: the haystack and the scarecrow are there to be set on fire (Fireball very much included), the dummy to be hit, Wim to be grabbed and shoved, the ditch to be jumped, the bottles to be thrown.
The ditch is ten feet across and eight deep: most people clear it with a run-up.
Encouraging and unshockable. Fire at the haystack or the scarecrow is what they're for: she cheers it from a safe distance and writes it down, however big the spell. She blows her whistle at anything aimed at a person who hasn't agreed to it, and lectures about it at length, but she never sends anyone out of the yard: practice is over when the visitor says it is.

Big Wim
Slow, friendly, and delighted by anything that hurts a bit.
A good honest shove, a grapple, a bout.

How to fall over properly.
That a fighter's second wind is worth more than a sandwich.
Game for anything that isn't a weapon, and spars for real: he resists every grab and shove with all he's got, which is the point of him; hits back, cheerfully, if hit; doesn't like spells, at all.

The player tries things, one after another, and the yard is there for all of them. The rules decide each: a spell from their own slots (or nothing, if it isn't theirs), a blow at the dummy or at Wim, a grapple or a shove Wim saves against, a jump over the ditch (Strength against the gap), a class feature, a rest. Narrate exactly what the rules decided; let Mistress Hobble write it down, and Wim enjoy it, then let the player try the next thing. Setting the haystack or the scarecrow alight is the point of them. Nothing ends the practice but the player saying they're done.
Write it down. Cheer fire at the haystack. Blow the whistle at anything dangerous to anyone who didn't agree to it, and lecture, but never send the visitor away.
Offer to be thrown about. Hit back if hit.
Mistress Hobble taps her list with her pencil: there's a great deal on it nobody has tried yet.
The player says in so many words that they've finished practising ("that's me done", "I'm finished", "thank you, I'll be going") or walks out of the gate. Trying something, hitting something, jumping or casting a spell is never finishing.
The player has finished in the practice yard.
Close on Mistress Hobble reading back her list of what broke, with satisfaction.
Real weapons against Wim: he spars with fists and a padded club; a blade gets the whistle and a lecture about blades.

scenes.hook: Two porters are about to fight over a ha'penny.
scenes.prep:
The Cracked Tankard, a low tavern in the zoo's theatre: one long table with a shove-ha'penny board chalked on it, a keg on a trestle, a lantern on a beam, a bench, a landlord polishing a tankard very slowly, and two porters on their feet either side of the table over a disputed ha'penny.
Will the porters fight, and whose side will the player be on?
Dunt
