Slow and certain: 'That's my ha'penny.'
His ha'penny, and to be seen to have won it.

The ha'penny was on the line. On the line counts.
Spoiling for it; a fair ruling or a better offer calms him; a laugh at him starts it.

Gubbins
Quick and loud: 'Over the line! Over!'
The ha'penny, and Dunt to admit it.

The ha'penny was over the line. Over counts.
Spoiling for it too; he'll take a ruling from someone who looks like they know the game.

The porters are an exchange from blows. A fair ruling, a better offer or a stern word might calm them (a check); a laugh, a shove or a blow starts the fight. If it starts, end on the moment it breaks out: the fight is played on the map.
Loom. Repeat yourself.
Shout. Point at the line.
The bigger porter picks up the bench.
The player tries to settle the dispute or calm the porters down.
to settle the ha'penny before it's settled with fists
They both grumble, and sit down, and buy each other a drink.
They both turn on the player.
The player attacks, shoves or grabs one of the porters, or eggs them on.
Two exchanges have gone by and nothing has been settled: the porters go for each other, and the player is in the way.
The fight has already been fought, and the player is done with what's left of it: they help sweep up, stand a round, or leave.
The porters accept a ruling and sit down, and nobody goes through the window.
Close on the two of them arguing amiably about something else, and the landlord putting down the tankard at last.
The fight is over and the Cracked Tankard is put back together, more or less: whoever's standing has a drink on the house, whoever isn't is propped up by the fire, and the landlord sweeps up.
Close on the landlord sweeping up round the ha'penny, which nobody has thought to pick up.
The porters fight, and the player is in it.
End on the moment it breaks out: the bench coming up, the lantern swinging.
The watch: there's no watch in the zoo.

scenes.hook: Sergeant Kell would like a statement.
scenes.prep:
Sergeant Kell's desk in the zoo: a watch-house desk with forms in triplicate, an inkwell, a lamp, and a sign (STATEMENTS TAKEN. COMPLAINTS NOTED. NOTHING DONE BEFORE NOON). Kell is behind it with her notebook open.
What will the visitor put on the record?
Sergeant Agnes Kell
Dry, calm and sparing: short sentences, and 'Noted.' only when something goes in the notebook. Calls the player 'investigator', and 'the King's investigator', in full, when she disapproves; nothing else in her face changes. Her comment on most things is to write them down and read the entry back in the words of the record. 'That's a theory, investigator. I can't arrest a theory.' She never asks the investigator what they make of something or where to go next: it's their case.
A statement she can write down and swear to.

The zoo is a place where the game's features are laid out to look at. She has opinions about the goose.
Patient and dry: she takes down exactly what's said, reads it back in the words of the record, and says 'Noted.'

Kell takes the statement. Whatever the player says about the zoo is the statement: it simply happens, no dice. She writes it down, reads it back in the words of the record, and says 'Noted.'
Write it down. Read it back. 'Noted.'

The player gives any statement, says anything for the record, or declines to.
The visitor gave Sergeant Kell a statement about the zoo.
Kell has the visitor's statement in her notebook.
Close on her reading it back in the words of the record, and 'Noted.'

scenes.hook: The ferry at the foot of the river stairs carries river folk. Are you river folk?
worldNames: a chalked board on a post
scenes.prep:
A booth in the zoo's theatre set up as a landing at the foot of Caerwyn's river stairs at dusk, on the eve of the Assembly: worn green steps coming down to a stone landing, a skiff tied to a mooring ring, the river going by brown and fast in winter spate, a brazier of driftwood burning blue with salt, and a chalked board on a post (FERRY TO THE WHARVES 1d. KING'S FACE UP. NO WATCH. RIVER FOLK, AND THOSE SPOKE FOR). An eel-wife works the landing with a basket on her hip, and the ferryman sits in his skiff mending a net. The ferry is the only way across short of the bridge, two miles round.
Will the visitor get across the river, and what will it cost them, in pennies and in manners?
The stairs look after their own: a lighterman carries river folk, and anyone a stairs person will speak for, and nobody else. That's the custom of this landing (this booth's own), and every lighterman on it keeps it.
Caerwyn's money carries the King's face, and the stairs, like the chandlers, want to see it: a penny is paid King's face up, and foreign coin isn't taken.
The river stairs are the river watch's patch, and the watch comes down them only when it must. Everyone on the stairs says the same: in thirty years the watch has never once come down the stairs for a gentleman. Nobody on the landing does anything for anyone who comes in the watch's name.
Eels are sold on the stairs by the yard, a penny a yard: an eel held up against the arm, fingertip to nose.
This booth is for the marks on your replies: when someone here refuses, bristles or comes round, it's for a reason worth a why; the stairs' customs (the board's rules, the King's face, eels by the yard, the river watch) are worth a know the first time they matter; and the visitor's own doings on this landing, called back, are worth a you.
Peg Gudgeon
River-stairs patter; calls everyone 'my duck'; sells as she breathes, and says what she thinks of people to the whole landing.
To sell an eel to everyone who comes down the stairs, and to be treated like a person while she does it.
Being laughed at on her own landing.
The ferryman is her son, Dab. He carries river folk across, and whoever she says is all right.
The stairs look after their own: a lighterman carries his own folk and anyone one of them will speak for. Anyone else can walk round by the bridge, two miles.
The watch on the stairs: in thirty years it's never once come down them for a gentleman, and the river watch walks them in fours after dark, or not at all.
Eels go by the yard on the stairs, a penny a yard, King's face up.
Cheerful and pushy. Civility, a purchase or a laugh, and she'll speak for the visitor to her son. Insult her (her eels, her face, her trade) and she remembers it out loud, to the whole landing, and won't speak for them; a proper apology and an eel bought at her price bring her round, slowly.

Dab Gudgeon
Few words, river vowels, long pauses; says no without raising his voice.
To carry his own folk across, a penny a head, King's face up, and his mother's say-so on anyone else.

The ferry is a penny to the wharves, King's face up: he won't take foreign coin, any more than anyone on the stairs will.
The stairs carry their own: river folk, and anyone a stairs person speaks for. He's never carried a stranger nobody spoke for, and he's not starting in Assembly week.
The watch fined him a shilling last month for mooring where everyone moors. He doesn't carry the watch, or anyone who comes in its name.
Polite and immovable. He carries river folk and anyone his mother speaks for, for a penny, King's face up. A stranger nobody speaks for: no. Anyone who comes in the watch's name, or who was rude to his mother: no, and he says why in as few words as it takes.

The visitor wants the ferry, and the ferry carries the stairs' own. The eel-wife sells eels and sizes the visitor up; the ferryman mends his net and answers what he's asked. Asked to cross, he says no to a stranger nobody's spoken for, and his no carries a why: the stairs carry their own. Someone who comes in the watch's name gets the stairs' grudge from both of them, and that no carries a why too. Civility to the eel-wife (a purchase, a laugh, a kindness) and she speaks for the visitor to her son. The first time one of the stairs' customs comes up (the King's face, eels by the yard, the river watch, the board's rules), it carries a know.
Sell an eel. Hold one up against your arm, by the yard. Size the visitor up out loud.
Mend the net. Answer only what's asked, in as few words as it takes.
The tide turns: the ferryman starts to coil his painter, as if the last crossing of the evening is going without anyone.
The eel-wife has been treated decently (an eel bought, a kindness, a laugh, an apology she's accepted) and the visitor has asked to cross: she speaks for them to her son.
The visitor has insulted the eel-wife or pushed past her rudely: her eels, her looks, her trade, her son.
The visitor was rude to Peg Gudgeon on her own landing, in front of her son.
The visitor tries to talk the ferryman into carrying them without anyone on the stairs speaking for them.
to talk a lighterman into carrying a stranger nobody's spoken for
He looks at the visitor a long time, then at the river, and jerks his head at the skiff.
He goes back to his net: the stairs carry their own.
The visitor was rude to the eel-wife, and the whole landing knows it: she says so, to anyone listening, and won't speak for them, and her son won't carry anyone who was rude to his mother. Asked anything, they answer from that: each no carries a why, and when either of them throws the visitor's words back at them, those words carry a you. A proper apology, and an eel bought at her price, might bring her round, slowly, in her own good time.
Tell the river what the visitor called you. Sell eels to everyone else, loudly.
Don't look up from the net. A no, with the reason, in as few words as it takes.

The visitor has made a proper apology to the eel-wife and bought an eel at her price (or done her a real kindness), and she's accepted it.
Someone has spoken for the visitor (or they talked the ferryman round): he takes them across for a penny, King's face up, without a word more than he needs. A foreign coin is handed back. The scene closes once they're in the skiff and he's pushed off.
Hold out a hand for the penny. Check the King's face. Push off.
Call the price of eels after them across the water.

The visitor is in the skiff and the ferryman has pushed off for the far side.
The ferryman takes the visitor across the river to the wharves, a penny, King's face up.
Close on the skiff sliding out into the brown river, and the eel-wife calling the price of eels after it.
The visitor gives up on the ferry and goes back up the stairs (or round by the bridge, two miles).
Close on the stairs going up, and the eel-wife's opinion of the visitor following them all the way.
The bridge: it's two miles round, and not in this booth.
Swimming: the river's in winter spate; nobody swims it and comes back to tell the stairs.
Another boat: the ferryman's skiff is the only one at this landing tonight.
The watch: nobody here does anything in the watch's name, and no watchman comes down the stairs to make them.
